body.objective: Students will be able to draw with contour and gesture.
body.iCan: I can draw with contour and gesture.
successCriteria: I can draw quick gesture drawings that capture movement

body.hook: Most people draw what they think something looks like, not what they actually see. A gesture drawing takes 30 seconds and captures energy; a contour drawing takes 10 minutes and captures every edge. Together they train your eye to see like an artist.

vocabulary.definition: A quick, loose drawing that captures the movement and energy of a subject.
A line that follows the edges and surface changes of a form.

study.title: Seeing Like an Artist
study.question: How do gesture and contour drawing help me really see?
study.passage:
Part 1, Gesture warm-up (10 minutes): A classmate holds short poses (30 seconds, then 1 minute, then 2 minutes). Draw the whole figure with loose, continuous lines. Start with the line of action, a curve showing the main direction of the pose.
Part 2, Blind contour (10 minutes): Draw your non-drawing hand or a shoe without looking at the paper. Move your eyes and pencil slowly at the same speed along every edge. The result will look strange; that's the point. You're training your eye, not making a finished drawing.
Part 3, Modified contour (20 minutes): Draw a still life (a backpack, a plant, a crumpled bag). Look at the paper only to place your pencil. Vary line quality: press harder for edges closer to you or in shadow, lighter for distant or lit edges.
Part 4, Sighting: hold your pencil at arm's length, close one eye, and compare the height and width of the object before drawing.
Reflection: Compare your first and last drawings. What do you notice now that you missed before?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to measure proportion by sight.
body.iCan: I can measure proportion by sight.
successCriteria: I can use sighting to compare sizes and angles
I can find proportions using a unit of measure
I can correct a drawing by checking proportions
body.hook: Draw a friend's face and the eyes often end up near the top of the head. In reality, eyes sit about halfway down. Artists don't guess proportions; they measure them by sight with a pencil held at arm's length.

vocabulary.definition: The size of one part compared to another part or the whole.
Measuring by holding a pencil at arm's length to compare sizes and angles.
One part of the subject used to measure all the others, such as the height of a head.
When an object pointing toward the viewer looks shorter than it really is.
An imaginary vertical line used to check alignment.
The space around and between objects.

study.title: Measure with Your Eye
study.question: How do artists measure proportion by sight?
study.passage:
Sighting method: Stand in the same spot, arm fully straight, one eye closed. Hold the pencil vertically or horizontally. Line the tip up with one edge of an object and slide your thumb to the other edge. That length is your unit.
Part 1, Practice (10 minutes): Sight a classroom door. How many door widths fit in its height? (Often about two and a half.) Check with a tape measure afterwards.
Part 2, Still life (25 minutes): Set up a bottle, a mug and a box. Choose the mug's height as the unit. Sight: How many mugs tall is the bottle? How wide is the box in mug units? Mark these on your paper lightly before drawing. Use the pencil to check angles of tilted edges, and use plumb lines to see what lines up vertically.
Part 3, Figure proportions (10 minutes): An adult standing figure is about seven and a half heads tall. The eyes are halfway down the head. The elbows line up with the waist; the fingertips reach mid-thigh. Sketch a classmate posing for two minutes using head units.
Part 4, Check (5 minutes): Turn your drawing upside down or look in a mirror. Errors jump out. Correct one.

body.objective: Students will be able to render form with value.
body.iCan: I can render form with value.
successCriteria: I can identify the parts of light on a form
I can render a form using a full value range
I can use hatching, cross-hatching and blending
body.hook: A circle on paper is flat. Add a shadow, a highlight and a little reflected light, and suddenly it's a ball you could pick up. That's the power of value: the range from light to dark that makes forms look three-dimensional.

vocabulary.definition: How light or dark a tone is.
The brightest spot where light hits directly.
The darkest part of the shadow on the form itself.
The shadow a form throws onto a nearby surface.
Light bounced back onto the shadow side from nearby surfaces.
Shading a drawing to show form, light and texture.

study.title: Light on Form
study.question: How does value turn flat shapes into 3-D forms?
study.passage:
Materials: 2H, HB, 2B and 6B pencils; blending stump; kneaded eraser; white egg, ball or cylinder; one desk lamp.
Part 1, Parts of light (10 minutes): Light one white ball from one side. Find and label: highlight, light side, half-tone (mid value), core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow. Note: the cast shadow is darkest right where the ball touches the table.
Part 2, Value scale (10 minutes): Make a 7-step scale from white to the darkest dark. Make one with hatching (parallel lines), one with cross-hatching and one blended.
Part 3, Render (25 minutes): Draw the egg or ball lit by the lamp. Lightly map the shapes of light and shadow first, then build values gradually from light to dark. Keep the highlight as clean paper. Lift highlights with a kneaded eraser if needed. Shade reflected light lighter than the core shadow but darker than the light side.
Part 4, Critique (5 minutes): Squint at your drawing beside the real object. Squinting simplifies values. Is your darkest dark dark enough?

practice.q: How does the cast shadow show the light direction?
